claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and degradation.
High entropy of mixing enhances formation or effectiveness of the stable oxide layer.
Mixing the alloy elements increases configurational entropy.
The increase in configurational entropy reduces the Gibbs free energy of the system.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloys have a uniform elemental distribution and crystalline structure.
Heating at 800°C in argon will produce a stable surface oxide layer at least 5 nm thick.
Surface oxide formation is driven by reaction of alloy elements with oxygen.
The combined oxide-layer and entropy mechanism maintains structural and chemical stability.
Heating will yield a 30% increase in stability relative to untreated nanoalloys.
Stability can be measured through the percentages of retained crystalline structure and retained uniform elemental distribution.
The prediction applies from 700°C to 900°C in argon for crystalline high-entropy nanoalloys with initially uniform elemental distributions.
The selected heating rate of 10°C/min and two-hour hold are based on previous oxide-layer formation studies.
Exact alloy composition and the type of inert atmosphere may affect oxide-layer formation and stability.
Failure to form an oxide layer at least 5 nm thick would falsify the hypothesis.
A stability increase below 20% would falsify the hypothesis.
